questions.q: Why can an open redirect bypass an SSRF URL filter?
o: The redirect encrypts the internal URL so the filter cannot see it
The filter checks only the first URL, then the client follows redirects
The redirect turns off the server HTTP client for that whole request
The attacker must log in first before the filter will allow the URL
questions.x: The filter asks whether the initial URL looks safe, often because it is on the victim host. It does not evaluate the Location the HTTP client follows next, so the second hop can be localhost or another blocked target.
questions.h: The filter sees the URL you submit. After a 302, who chooses the next hop, and does the filter run again?

questions.q: Why does the first URL in this chain look safe to the filter?
o: It is always HTTPS, and every filter allows any HTTPS URL
It points at the victim site, which passes an allowlist check
It hides the internal IP inside a long base64 path segment
It uses DNS rebinding so the resolved IP changes after the check
questions.x: Direct internals like http://localhost/admin are blocked. A URL such as https://victim/redirect?url=http://localhost/admin is still on an allowed host, so the first-hop check passes.
questions.h: The filter is asking 'is this first URL external and allowed?' What does the victim's own redirect endpoint look like to that check?

questions.q: What job does the open redirect endpoint do in this chain?
o: It issues the SSRF fetch from the attacker's own browser tab
It 302s the server's follow-up request onto the internal target
It stores admin credentials for the attacker to collect later
It encrypts the SSRF body before the server sends the request
questions.x: The open redirect is a proxy in the redirect sense. The server's HTTP client requested an allowed URL, received a redirect to the internal admin path, and followed it. The attacker browser never needed to reach that admin interface.
questions.h: The redirect endpoint does not fetch the internal URL for the attacker. It tells the server's HTTP client where to go next.

questions.q: What does the SSRF filter fail to inspect in this attack?
o: The HTTP method used on the first outbound request
The final URL after the HTTP client follows the redirect
The Host header value on the attacker-supplied first URL
The Content-Type header of the product stock API response
questions.x: Most server HTTP libraries follow 3xx responses by default. The filter already approved the first URL. The client then lands on an internal address the filter would have rejected if it had been submitted directly.
questions.h: There are two URLs in play: the one submitted and the one after the 302. Which of those did the filter never see?

questions.q: What is the result of a successful SSRF plus open-redirect chain?
o: The attacker browser loads the internal admin page directly
The server reaches an internal URL the filter would have blocked
The open redirect stores the admin HTML in a public cache
The filter is disabled for every later request in that session
questions.x: The server-side fetch follows the victim redirect onto the internal admin interface. That is the SSRF the first-hop filter was meant to stop. The filter still only ran on the allowed external URL.
questions.h: Who actually connects to localhost or the internal admin path, the attacker browser or the vulnerable server?
